# Cardiac Contractility Modulation Therapy for Heart Failure: A Narrative Review

## Introduction

Heart failure (HF) remains a major source of morbidity and mortality despite advances in guideline-directed medical therapy (GDMT). Device-based therapies such as cardiac resynchronization therapy (CRT) and implantable cardioverter-defibrillators improve outcomes only in selected patients—principally those with a wide QRS complex—leaving the majority of patients with HF and reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF) without a disease-modifying device option [1]. Cardiac contractility modulation (CCM) was developed to address this gap. CCM applies precisely timed electrical signals to the ventricular myocardium during refractoriness, thereby influencing myocardial performance without generating an additional depolarization [2].

## Mechanism of Action

CCM signals are delivered to the right ventricular septum through transvenous leads connected to an implantable pulse generator. CCM delivers a biphasic high-voltage signal (7.5 V/22-ms duration) to the right ventricular septum during the absolute refractory period; when administered for 5–12 h/day, this device acutely augments dP/dt without raising oxygen consumption, thereby improving cardiac efficiency [3]. The hemodynamic benefit is multifactorial. These signals have been shown to have myocardial effects within minutes to hours in the region near the stimulation electrodes, including phosphorylation of key proteins involved with calcium cycling and contractile proteins and shifts of myocardial gene expression from a fetal genotype typical of chronic heart failure to a more normal adult genotype; over time, these effects are evident in regions remote from the stimulation site [4]. Mechanistic work has clarified the underlying biology. CCM signals, consisting of biphasic high-voltage bipolar signals delivered to the right ventricular septum during the absolute refractory period, have been shown to improve symptoms, exercise tolerance and quality of life and reduce the rate of HF hospitalizations in patients with ejection fractions between 25% and 45% [5]. Preclinical studies in dogs with chronic HF demonstrated that long-term delivery of CCM electric signals improves LV function and global, cellular, and molecular remodeling, after acute studies showed CCM signals applied to the failing myocardium during the absolute refractory period improved LV function without increasing myocardial oxygen consumption [6]. The favorable oxygen-consumption profile was confirmed in human studies [7].

## Clinical Evidence

The earliest randomized trial, FIX-HF-4, established proof of concept. This randomized, double-blind, crossover study of CCM signals enrolled 164 subjects with ejection fraction < 35% and NYHA Class II or III symptoms who received a CCM pulse generator [8]. The pivotal FIX-HF-5 study followed. In this prospective, unblinded, randomized, parallel-group, controlled trial, 428 patients were randomly assigned to receive optimal medical therapy plus CCM (n = 215) versus OMT alone (n = 213) [9,10]. That study met its primary safety endpoint, but the primary efficacy endpoint—a responders' analysis of changes in ventilatory anaerobic threshold—was not met [11]. However, it showed significant improvements in the secondary endpoints of peak VO2 and Minnesota Living With Heart Failure Questionnaire score, and was the first to show that patients with an LVEF between 35% and 45% benefited the most, whereas those with EF < 25% derived less benefit [12].

This signal prompted the confirmatory FIX-HF-5C trial. A total of 160 participants with NYHA class III or IV symptoms and LVEF 25–45% were randomized to continue OMT or receive CCM for 24 weeks, and the primary efficacy endpoint was met with a peak oxygen-uptake difference between groups of 0.84 ml O2/kg/min [13]. Secondary outcomes, including the MLWHFQ, NYHA functional class, and 6-minute walk test, were all significantly better in the treatment group [13]. The system was subsequently simplified: prior studies employed a 3-lead Optimizer system, but a new 2-lead system eliminated the need for an atrial lead, and the FIX-HF-5C2 study tested the safety and effectiveness of this 2-lead system [14]. A pooled individual-patient-data meta-analysis subsequently strengthened the evidence base. Giallauria and colleagues performed a comprehensive individual patient data meta-analysis of all randomized trials and the nonrandomized FIX-HF-5C2, including 861 patients, and showed that CCM significantly improved peak VO2, 6-minute walk test distance, and quality of life [15].

## Real-World and Long-Term Outcomes

Registry data support durability of benefit. CCM-REG is a prospective registry study including 503 patients from 51 European centres assessing long-term effects on quality of life, LVEF, mortality, and hospitalizations [16]. CCM improved functional status, quality of life, and LVEF and, compared with patients' prior history, reduced HF hospitalization rates, with survival at 1 and 3 years significantly better than predicted by the MAGGIC risk score [16,17]. An earlier registry analysis similarly reported improved long-term survival and reduced hospitalizations in HFrEF [18]. Single-center series have corroborated these findings [19], and earlier feasibility and lead-configuration studies established the safety profile [20,21].

## Expanding Indications

CCM is increasingly studied beyond classic HFrEF. Mechanistic work suggests dysregulated calcium handling is common across the EF spectrum [22], and CCM has been explored for HF with preserved ejection fraction. The CCM-HFpEF pilot study reported that CCM therapy improves health status in patients with HFpEF [23], although these results need to be corroborated in a randomized controlled clinical trial across a longer follow-up period, and the AIM HIGHer pivotal trial has been initiated to do so [23]. The therapy also appears effective in patients with moderately prolonged QRS, where CCM significantly improved HF control in NYHA class III HFrEF patients with QRSd of 120–149 ms, comparable to that in patients with QRS < 120 ms [24]. Earlier reviews summarized the evolving rationale for CCM as a complement to GDMT [25,26].

## Regulatory and Guideline Status

Two seminal clinical trials, FIX-HF-5 and FIX-HF-5C, resulted in the 2019 breakthrough FDA approval of the Optimizer Smart System CCM device for patients with NYHA class III HF with LVEF of 25% to 45% [27]. The discussion of CCM devices was first included in the European Society of Cardiology HF guidelines in 2016 and is mentioned in the 2022 ACC/AHA guidelines for the management of HF [28,29]. Current ESC guidance positions CCM as a therapy under evaluation for selected symptomatic patients [30].

## Conclusion

CCM provides a mechanistically distinct, well-tolerated device option that improves exercise capacity, symptoms, and quality of life in symptomatic HFrEF (and HFmrEF) patients ineligible for CRT. Robust mortality data remain limited, and ongoing randomized trials—including studies in HFmrEF and HFpEF—will define its ultimate role.
